items.title: Your muscles cannot share their sugar reserves with your brain
items.claim: Your body stores carbohydrate as glycogen. The liver holds ~100 grams; skeletal muscle ~400 grams. The liver's glycogen feeds the blood and brain. Muscle glycogen is for muscle's own use — it cannot release glucose to the bloodstream.
items.prompt: Why can the liver release glucose to blood but muscle cannot?

options.text: Muscle is too far from blood vessels

Liver expresses glucose-6-phosphatase, the enzyme that removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate so glucose can leave the cell; skeletal muscle does not have this enzyme, so the breakdown product is trapped and used locally

items.reveal:
Glycogen breakdown:
1. Glycogen phosphorylase clips glucose-1-phosphate off the glycogen chain.
2. Phosphoglucomutase converts it to glucose-6-phosphate.
3. To leave the cell, the phosphate must be removed (glucose can cross membranes, but glucose-6-phosphate cannot).

Liver and kidney have glucose-6-phosphatase — they CAN remove the phosphate and export free glucose into the blood, supplying the brain and red blood cells.

Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. The glucose-6-phosphate must be used locally — typically immediately entering glycolysis for ATP production.

The Cori cycle compensates indirectly: muscle generates lactate (during anaerobic exertion), exports it to the liver, where it's converted back to glucose (gluconeogenesis) and shipped back to muscle.

Von Gierke's disease (glycogen storage disease type I) is an inherited deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase: even liver glycogen cannot be exported. Patients have severe fasting hypoglycaemia.

Liver glycogen depletes in ~24 hours of fasting; muscle glycogen depletes in ~90 minutes of hard exercise. After that, fat and (eventually) protein become the energy source.
items.why: Sugar storage feels like a shared pool. It isn't — the body has specialised tissue-level energy compartments, controlled by which enzymes each tissue expresses.

items.title: Your kidneys filter 180 litres of blood plasma every day
items.claim: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Together they filter 125 ml of plasma per minute — 180 litres per day. Your final urine output is 1 to 2 litres. The kidneys reabsorb 99% of what they filter.
items.prompt: Why filter so much only to put it back?

options.text: Bulk filtration is the only way to expose all blood-borne solutes to selective reabsorption; the kidney keeps what's needed (glucose, salts, amino acids, water) and lets the rest go — fine selectivity requires high throughput
The body has extra water to spare

items.reveal:
The glomerulus is a knot of capillaries inside a Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure forces plasma (minus proteins and cells) through a selective barrier into the nephron tubule.

Flow rates: glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ~120-125 ml/min in healthy adults. Total renal blood flow ~1.2 L/min — about 20-25% of cardiac output. The kidneys take a major share of the circulation for their mass.

The filtrate then passes through the tubules. Proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, most salts, water. Loop of Henle sets up an osmotic gradient. Distal tubule fine-tunes. Collecting duct adjusts water under ADH (antidiuretic hormone).

Result: 180 L filtered, 178.5 L returned to blood, 1.5 L excreted as urine.

GFR drops with age (~1% per year after 40), kidney disease, dehydration. Maintaining it is why drinking water matters — and why drugs that affect kidney function require careful monitoring.
items.why: Filtration that throws everything out and re-claims most of it sounds wasteful. It's the simplest design that ensures any potentially harmful blood-borne molecule eventually leaves the body.

items.title: You are paralysed multiple times every night
items.claim: During REM sleep, when most dreams occur, motor neurons to your skeletal muscles are actively inhibited. You cannot move. This is REM atonia — and when it fails, people act out their dreams.
items.prompt: Why does the brain paralyse you while dreaming?

options.text: To prevent acting out dream content — the same brain regions that command movement are active in REM as in waking, but spinal motor neurons are blocked from receiving the signals
To stop heart rate from rising

items.reveal_title: REM behavior disorder and Schenck's discovery
items.reveal:
The brainstem (specifically the pons and medulla) sends inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons during REM. The motor cortex fires in patterns resembling waking; the descending commands reach the spinal cord but cannot trigger muscle contraction.

In REM Behavior Disorder (Schenck 1986), this paralysis fails. Patients punch, kick, vocalise and act out vivid dreams. RBD is strongly associated with later Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia — the brainstem regions controlling REM atonia degrade early in these conditions.

Narcolepsy with cataplexy is the opposite failure: REM-style atonia intrudes into waking life, triggered by emotion. Modafinil and other treatments stabilise the boundary between sleep states.
items.why: Sleep is imagined as 'off'. REM sleep is intensely active — and the body needs active suppression to prevent the brain's instructions reaching the muscles.
